headline: Accountingbpo turned a headcount-bound accounting back office into a supervised AI workflow.

metrics.label: Accounting document processing time
metrics.attribution: Company-reported; published in the IMDA/SBF award citation

metrics.label: Management reporting
metrics.attribution: Company-reported; published in the IMDA/SBF award citation

metrics.label: Administrative coordination
metrics.attribution: Company-reported; published in the IMDA/SBF award citation

scqa.s: Accountingbpo is a Singapore professional services firm and business process outsourcing provider. It delivers tech-enabled financial management, corporate compliance and digital accounting workflows for client companies. The delivery model depends on two scarce resources: people who can read financial documents accurately, and people who can coordinate many client engagements at once. Both scale with volume, so growth historically meant hiring.
scqa.c: The award citation names three constraints. Manual data entry and reconciliation created heavy administrative work and delayed the completion of accounts. Assignments and client information were spread across separate documents, and coordination alone consumed about 400 hours each month. Higher client volumes therefore required more manpower, which capped scalability and compressed margins. The cost of growth was linear in headcount, and every additional engagement added coordination overhead before it added margin. The firm could not promise a faster turnaround without hiring, and hiring reduced the margin on the work that funded it.
scqa.q: How could the firm process more client documents and coordinate more engagements without adding proportional headcount, while keeping a qualified accountant's approval over every financial output?
scqa.a: The firm built Yi.Suite, an integrated ecosystem of specialised AI tools organised around its accounting workflow. Automated document processing extracts information from invoices, suggests ledger accounts and matches vendors, and handles both batch and single-document intake. A coordination layer converts client emails into trackable work tickets, recommends task assignments and drafts context-aware replies. Reconciliation matches bank transactions against accounting records and drafts receivables follow-up. Business owners can query financial data in plain language and receive KPI summaries and dashboards. Financial statement preparation compiles drafts and verifies documents, with accountants reviewing and approving the outputs. Human judgement stays at the approval boundary rather than at the data-entry boundary. The citation reports up to 67% less document processing time, up to 16 times faster management reporting, and 396 manhours a month redirected from coordination to client work. The citation does not report error rates, and it does not describe how the firm validates extraction accuracy, so the quality effect of the change remains unquantified. The reporting multiple is the more durable of the two speed figures, because management reporting is repeatable work with a fixed shape, while document processing time depends on the mix of client documents and will move as volumes change.

takeaway: Automate the data entry, supervise the judgement. Put the accountant's approval after the AI's draft, not after the AI's extraction.

headline: Best Marketing Agency rebuilt its agency operating model around AI agents, and revenue per employee rose 71%.

metrics.label: Revenue per employee
metrics.attribution: Company-reported; published in the IMDA/SBF award citation

metrics.label: Delivery capacity per head
metrics.attribution: Company-reported; published in the IMDA/SBF award citation

metrics.label: Routine work
metrics.attribution: Company-reported; published in the IMDA/SBF award citation

scqa.s: Best Marketing Agency provides digital marketing services in Singapore, including search engine optimisation, paid advertising, social media management and content creation. Agency economics depend on the ratio between billable output and the coordination required to produce it. Every additional client adds reporting, finance administration and internal handoffs before it adds margin.
scqa.c: Client delivery, reporting, finance and internal operations sat in separate tools, spreadsheets and chat threads. Account managers spent about two working days per client each month preparing reports alone. Finance and other administrative processes were also manual. The citation links manual coordination to high overheads and to senior staff being pulled away from sales, strategy and client engagement. The firm was paying specialist salaries for coordination work. Growth therefore added cost at roughly the same rate as revenue, which kept margin flat regardless of how many clients the agency won.
scqa.q: How could the agency raise output per person without lowering delivery quality or losing human control over client-facing and financial decisions?
scqa.a: The agency built Big Beast, an AI-powered operating system that connects delivery, reporting, finance and internal operations in one platform. AI agents execute routine processes, and human approval is retained for consequential actions. Automated reporting pulls advertising and search data, tracks keyword performance and generates campaign summaries and live reports. Finance workflows automate invoicing, bank reconciliation and accounting, with approval gates on financial actions. Operations bring task management, payroll, CPF computation, HR processes and contract e-signing together. Content agents draft search copy, advertisements and landing pages, with automated quality and compliance checks supporting human review. Lead routing, unanswered-enquiry flags and renewal-risk detection use campaign and payment records. The citation reports a 71% increase in revenue per employee, a 73% increase in delivery capacity per head, and 1,000 staff-hours saved from routine work each month. The company also publishes its own account of the award, which names Big Beast and describes a 24/7 AI salesperson for lead qualification. The citation does not separate the contribution of the agents from other changes in the period, so the 71% figure should be read as the firm's own account of the combined effect. Revenue per employee is the right headline here, because it captures both the hours removed and the work retained, whereas delivery capacity per head could rise simply by lowering the standard of what is delivered.

takeaway: Measure revenue per employee, not tools deployed. The gain came from removing coordination work, not from drafting faster.

claims.text: Account managers spent around two working days per client each month preparing reports.
Big Beast embeds AI agents across workflows while retaining human approval for consequential actions.
The company states that it won the Innovation Excellence Trustmark for Big Beast.

headline: Blue Aqua put predictive AI on pond data and cut production cost by around 30%.

metrics.label: Production cost management
metrics.attribution: Company-reported; published in the IMDA/SBF award citation

metrics.label: Shrimp survival rate
metrics.attribution: Company-reported; published in the IMDA/SBF award citation

metrics.label: Manpower
metrics.attribution: Company-reported; published in the IMDA/SBF award citation

scqa.s: Blue Aqua International provides sustainable aquaculture, animal nutrition and farm management solutions to farmers worldwide. The Singapore Food Agency records that the company runs a local hatchery nurturing more than 100 million post-larval shrimp a year. Shrimp farming is a biological operation with thin margins: feed is a major cost, water conditions change faster than manual checks, and disease can spread through a pond before it is visible.
scqa.c: Water quality was checked infrequently, so problems could develop undetected between readings. Feeding was generic rather than matched to the pond, which wasted feed and money, and late disease detection raised the risk of stock loss. Decisions depended heavily on individual experience, paper logs and inconsistent records, which made performance hard to compare across farms. Expertise therefore did not scale: each farm's results depended on who was managing it. A farm manager's departure took the operating knowledge with them, and the company had no consistent way to compare one pond's performance against another.
scqa.q: How could the company convert scattered pond observations and individual experience into consistent, early warnings that any farm team could act on?
scqa.a: The company built AquaPilot, an aquaculture intelligence platform that analyses water quality, feeding, health and production data. It forecasts oxygen, ammonia and temperature six to 24 hours ahead using sensor and farm data, and alerts teams to emerging issues. It generates daily pond-level disease risk scores and flags potential health problems four to seven days before they usually become visible. Feed calculations are pond-specific and use biomass, water conditions, growth patterns and health risk. The system also monitors the recirculating aquaculture system, predicting issues and adjusting feeding in response. A benchmarking layer compares ponds on feed conversion, survival, growth and production cost, and returns farm-specific recommendations. The published result is a 30% improvement in production cost management, survival rates 6 to 9 percentage points higher, and around 2,500 manpower hours saved each year. The citation does not report model accuracy or the number of ponds covered, so the improvement cannot be separated from farm-level management changes. The survival-rate range is the more telling number, because it moves a biological outcome rather than a cost line, and biological outcomes are harder to attribute to any single management change than a feed bill is.

takeaway: The model is the easy part. The value sits in turning sensor readings into a daily decision that a farm hand can act on before the loss happens.

claims.text: Water quality was checked infrequently, so issues could go undetected between readings.
AquaPilot forecasts oxygen, ammonia and temperature six to 24 hours ahead.
The platform flags disease risk four to seven days before issues typically become visible.
Blue Aqua runs a Singapore hatchery that nurtures over 100 million post-larval shrimp a year.
claims.basis: Stated independently by the Singapore Food Agency.

headline: GetGo uses computer vision to attribute car damage to the right booking, recovering S$20,000 in two months.

metrics.label: Damage-to-invoice lead time
metrics.attribution: Company-reported; published in the IMDA/SBF award citation

metrics.label: Manual review workload
metrics.attribution: Company-reported; published in the IMDA/SBF award citation

metrics.label: Damage costs recovered
metrics.attribution: Company-reported; published in the IMDA/SBF award citation

scqa.s: GetGo Technologies runs an on-demand carsharing service on a pay-as-you-drive basis. A vendor case study published by Zendesk in 2024 records that the fleet exceeded 2,400 cars across more than 1,500 locations. Every rental begins and ends with photographs of the vehicle, taken by the customer. Those photographs are the only record of the vehicle's condition at the moment of handover.
scqa.c: The citation states that around 7,000 daily bookings generate about 56,000 end-trip photographs. Inspecting every booking manually is not feasible at that ratio. Damage could therefore go unnoticed until a customer reported it or a workshop found it days or weeks later. Late detection broke the link between damage and the booking that caused it, so the cost of repair could not be recovered from the responsible renter. The company carried the loss, and the invoice for damage arrived long after the rental ended. The company also carried the cost of disputes, because a charge raised weeks later is harder to defend than one raised at handover.
scqa.q: How could GetGo inspect tens of thousands of handover photographs a day, decide which booking caused any damage, and bill it accurately without accusing the wrong customer?
scqa.a: GetGo built Project Desmond, a damage detection system that combines computer vision, image matching and human validation. It analyses end-trip photographs and detects billable damage such as scratches, dents, cracks and dangling parts. It then compares consecutive bookings to establish when damage first appeared, and uses image embeddings to judge whether a detected defect is new or a recurring one already on file. Flagged cases route to human reviewers, who validate before any case proceeds to follow-up and billing. The model is retrained on real failure cases, including rain and reflections, to raise precision and cut false positives. The citation reports a 53% reduction in the lead time from damage to invoice, 60% less manual review work, and S$20,000 recovered in two months. The design keeps a person between the model and the customer, which matters when the output becomes a charge. The citation does not publish the model's precision or the dispute rate, so the commercial effect of a false positive is not documented. The recovered amount is a floor rather than a ceiling, because it measures only damage billed within two months, and says nothing about damage prevented, disputes avoided, or repairs found before a vehicle left the lot.

takeaway: When AI output becomes a bill, the review step is not overhead. It is the control that makes the automation usable.

claims.text: Around 7,000 daily bookings generate about 56,000 end-trip photographs.
Project Desmond uses image embeddings to determine whether damage is new or recurring across adjacent bookings.
AI-flagged cases route to human reviewers before billing.
GetGo operated more than 2,400 cars across more than 1,500 locations.
claims.basis: Stated in a Zendesk customer case study in 2024. The figure predates the award and concerns support operations, not damage detection.

headline: Glints cut internal fact-finding time by 90% with an agent that reads its own systems and source code.

metrics.label: Time spent fact-finding
metrics.attribution: Company-reported; published in the IMDA/SBF award citation

metrics.label: Specialist hours
metrics.attribution: Company-reported; published in the IMDA/SBF award citation

metrics.label: Staff time value
metrics.attribution: Company-reported; published in the IMDA/SBF award citation

scqa.s: Glints provides talent and managed workforce services across Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Vietnam, the Philippines and Taiwan. Its staff answer questions that cross borders: what a client was billed, which employee is assigned where, and what a given market's employment law requires. Each answer depends on a different system and a different jurisdiction.
scqa.c: Critical information sat across databases, business systems and the employment law of six markets. Routine questions needed help from Finance, Engineering or other specialists, and complex queries took hours or days. Repeated queries pulled specialists away from their own work. Worse, answers could differ between people and between markets, which created regulatory risk in an industry where an incorrect statement about pay or entitlement has consequences. The cost was not only time. It was the risk that two staff members would answer the same question differently in two markets.
scqa.q: How could staff get fast, consistent answers from company systems and six legal jurisdictions without queueing behind a specialist for every question?
scqa.a: Glints built Glimmer, a knowledge mining agent. Employees ask questions in plain language and the agent retrieves answers from company systems, internal knowledge, source code and employment law, showing the supporting sources. It pulls live client, employee, invoice and billing data from systems including NetSuite and HubSpot. It reads the company's source code to answer platform questions and provide first-line technical support before escalation. Governance is built into the retrieval: the system flags missing information, restricts citations to sources it actually accessed, and keeps audit logs. The citation reports a 90% reduction in fact-finding time, 1,700 specialist hours saved in six months, and S$120,000 of staff time saved each year. The design choice that matters is the citation constraint. An answer that must cite its source is auditable; an answer generated from general knowledge is not. The citation does not report how the agent handles a question that spans two jurisdictions, which is the hardest case in a six-market operation. The value of the agent compounds with market coverage, because every additional jurisdiction adds employment law that must be retrieved correctly rather than recalled from memory, and a wrong answer carries a regulatory cost.

takeaway: Constrain the agent to sources it actually read, and log the retrieval. In a regulated service, an uncited answer is a liability, not a feature.

Glimmer retrieves live client, employee, invoice and billing data from NetSuite and HubSpot.
The system flags missing information, restricts citations to accessed sources and maintains audit logs.
